reason: E2 states that alumina layers act as effective diffusion barriers in oxidative environments, but it explicitly notes these layers are unstable in molten fluoride salts and does not address molten aluminum. E1 discusses Al2O3 formation under hot corrosion by molten salts at 900°C, not molten aluminum at 660°C. Neither passage provides evidence that a preformed Al2O3 scale is stable, inert, or protective in molten aluminum, nor that it can be formed on boride-based components or remain adherent under the specified conditions.
premises: Alumina (Al2O3) is thermodynamically stable and chemically inert in contact with molten aluminum.
A dense, adherent Al2O3 layer acts as an effective diffusion barrier against further oxidation/corrosion.
Pre-oxidation can form a protective Al2O3 scale on a boride-based component.
The Al2O3 scale will remain intact and adherent under hot-dip aluminum plating conditions.
